To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(a) weight-sensitivity in English is not acquired by speakers of Mandarin or speakers of Portuguese, and that (b) this failure is due to a positional bias in the language.

(1) the positional bias in English is a confounding factor for second language acquisition, and (2) second language learners are not able to maintain weight-sensitivity in English, which is present in the input, due to the positional bias.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of input frequency in second language learning.
the following question: How does the L1 transfer into the L2?

the question of how second language learners of stress languages can acquire the correct generalizations about stress placement, and how they can avoid the confounding effects of other factors which may also be present in the L2 input.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the L1 transfer is only effective when there is no confounding factor in the target language, and when the learner has sufficient input.
second language learners of stress are sensitive to the positional bias in the target language and are not necessarily sensitive to the weight-sensitivity in it.
the learners’ responses to the English stress task reflect the combined effects of the L1, L2, and L3.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the L2 input does not always provide the necessary evidence for the learner to acquire the L1 pattern.
L2 transfer is not always effective, and the effectiveness depends on the relative strength of the factors in the L2 input.
L1 transfer can be obscured in L2 learning by confounding factors in L2 input.
The main takeaway from our work is that
L2 learners are more likely to acquire robust cues in their input rather than subtle cues which are not as prevalent in the input, even if the subtle cues are present in their L1.
second language learners are not necessarily more likely than native speakers to transfer L1 properties.
L1 transfer may not be effective in predicting second language acquisition patterns when there is confounding input.
